analysis.investment_thesis: Park Medi World has a respectable ROE of 21% and strong promoter holding, but at 44x P/E with D/E of 0.58 and a net profit CAGR of only 3.3% over four years, you are paying a premium price for very ordinary earnings growth. The business is accumulating debt faster than it is compounding profits, which violates my most basic principle.
key_strengths: High promoter holding at 82.89% — strong skin in the game and alignment
ROE/ROCE both above 20% — capital deployment has historically been reasonable
Healthcare demand in India is secular and defensive — NABH-accredited multi-specialty is a durable model
key_risks: Debt/Equity at 0.58 is a hard breach of my 0.3 ceiling — borrowings grew from ₹292 Cr to ₹734 Cr in 4 years
Finance costs CAGR 26.3% vs revenue CAGR 16.1% — debt is eating into earnings; net profit CAGR only 3.3%
FCF yield of ~0.7% (₹66 Cr FCF / ₹9,350 Cr market cap) — wildly inadequate for a value investor
red_flags: D/E 0.58 — crosses my unacceptable threshold of >0.5
Finance costs compounding at 26.3% per year — structural margin compression risk
Net profit fell from ₹228 Cr (FY23) to ₹152 Cr (FY24) — not the steady compounder I seek
Capex surged to ₹159 Cr in FY25 vs ₹71 Cr in FY24 — aggressive debt-funded expansion
P/E of 44x for a business with 3.3% net profit CAGR — valuation is simply unjustifiable
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Park Medi World has the surface features of a decent hospital chain — ROE above 20%, NABH accreditation, and a promoter who has not diluted. However, looking underneath, the earnings story is deeply disappointing. Revenue grew 16.1% CAGR but net profit managed only 3.3% CAGR from FY21 to FY25, with a sharp dip to ₹152 Cr in FY24. The culprit is plain: borrowings have ballooned from ₹292 Cr to ₹734 Cr and finance costs are compounding at 26.3% — absorbing most of the operating leverage that should have flowed to shareholders. This is the opposite of what I want in a business.

The valuation compounds the problem. At ₹9,350 Cr market cap against ₹66 Cr FCF in FY25, the FCF yield is less than 1% — I need at least 5%. P/E of 44x for a low-quality earnings trajectory is not a price I would pay for even the finest business in India, let alone one with a leveraged balance sheet and volatile cash flows. Unless the company shows sustained deleveraging and consistent double-digit profit growth, this is not a stock I would touch.
